## 6. lore — what 'freeya vidu' is actually made of

**ANNA:** what 'freeya vidu' is actually made of

**ANNA:** The word 'free' is inside it. Not borrowed loosely — it is doing real grammatical work.

**ANNA:** ஃப்ரீயா விடுங்க
> freeya vidu — release it into freedom

**ANNA:** The -யா suffix turns the noun into an adverb of manner. Freeya means 'in a free way', 'freely'. And vidu is let go, release, drop it.

**ANNA:** So the literal bones of it are: release this thing freely. Let it go free. Which is closer to what you mean than 'don't worry' ever quite captures.

**ANNA:** Now the other one. Kadaisil. It means at the end, at the last. But there is a texture in it that the translation loses.

**ANNA:** கடைசில பாக்கலாம்
> at the end, we'll see

**ANNA:** Paakalam is the permission form of see — we can see, we may see, we'll see. It is not a promise. It is not a refusal. It is a door left open by someone who has decided not to decide yet. The Coimbatore family uses it exactly where a plan would create pressure. Kadaisil paakalam is the phrase that keeps the room breathable.

## 12. lore — what 'room' holds in Tamil, and why the table already made space for you

**ANNA:** what 'room' holds in Tamil, and why the table already made space for you

**ANNA:** the word 'room' in English is about walls — four sides, a ceiling, a floor, a defined space you can step into and close off.

**ANNA:** Tamil doesn't reach for walls when it reaches for that idea. it reaches for something older — for whether there is enough.

**ANNA:** இடம்
> idam — place, space, room — but also standing, position, the fact that you belong somewhere

**ANNA:** when a Coimbatore household says there is idam at the table, they are not measuring square feet. they are saying you are accounted for. the space was always going to be there because you were always going to come.

**ANNA:** இன்னும் கொஞ்சம் சாப்பிடுங்க
> eat a little more — this is idam in action

**ANNA:** that line is not about food. it is the table telling you it made room — not just on the plate, but in the whole arrangement of the day. the cooking, the timing, the extra spoon of rice held back on purpose. idam was prepared before you arrived.

**ANNA:** சாஃப்ட்வேர் இன்ஜினியரா இருக்கேன்
> I'm a software engineer — the answer you give when someone is still working out your idam

**ANNA:** the moment that answer lands and they nod, the measuring is over. idam is confirmed. what comes next is just the meal.

## 18. lore — what கை கழுவிட்டு வரேன் actually contains

**ANNA:** what கை கழுவிட்டு வரேன் actually contains

**ANNA:** There is a whole philosophy of arrival inside this one phrase.

**ANNA:** கை கழுவிட்டு வரேன்
> hand-wash-having come — three acts compressed into one breath

**ANNA:** The literal pieces: கை is hand. கழுவி is the action of washing, mid-flight, not finished yet. வரேன் is I'm coming. But the order is the thing — you announce the washing before you do it, so the room knows you are already on your way back.

**ANNA:** In Coimbatore that phrase is not a request to wait. It is a promise with a shape. You are already considered present at the table. The washing is just the hinge between outside and in.

**ANNA:** A textbook would write it as a future tense sentence and move on. But what a Coimbatore ear hears is someone who already belongs at that table — someone who knows the meal is waiting, knows they are wanted, and names the one small act that separates them from sitting down.

**ANNA:** நீங்க சாப்பிட்டீங்களா
> the returning question — did you eat

**ANNA:** நீங்க is the respectful you — the one that bends toward an elder. சாப்பிட்டீங்களா folds the past tense and the question mark and the -nga of regard all into one word. You are not asking whether she is hungry. You are asking whether she was taken care of while you were gone. The question is really: did the room hold you well without me.

**ANNA:** These two phrases are a pair. One says I am coming back in. The other says I noticed you were here the whole time. Together they are how you re-enter a Tamil room — not with an announcement, but with your hands and your attention already given.

## 24. lore — what 'room' really means in Tamil

**ANNA:** what 'room' really means in Tamil

**ANNA:** There is no clean Tamil word for room. Not one that a Coimbatore house actually uses.

**ANNA:** The textbook will give you அறை. Old word, real word, means a divided-off space. But walk into his mother's house and ask

**ANNA:** தமிழ்ல எப்படி சொல்றது?
> how do you say it in Tamil

**ANNA:** and she will look at you sideways. Because she says room. Just room, slipped into Tamil the way a borrowed thing stops feeling borrowed after thirty years.

**ANNA:** This happens with a whole layer of the house. Hall. Kitchen. Room. The English words arrived with the floor plan — concrete walls, separate functions, a door on each one — and the Tamil just kept them.

**ANNA:** அறை didn't disappear. It went formal. You find it in paperwork, in songs, in the kind of sentence nobody actually speaks. And when you hear it in ordinary conversation, your first reaction is

**ANNA:** அப்படியா?!
> oh, is that so

**ANNA:** That mild surprise — because formal Tamil in a casual mouth sounds slightly out of place, the way a suit does at a family lunch. The word is right. The register is off.

## 30. lore — why 'change' and 'hurry' are the same kind of word

**ANNA:** why 'change' and 'hurry' are the same kind of word

**ANNA:** These two words look nothing alike. But they're built the same way, and once you hear it, you can't unhear it.

**ANNA:** சில்லறை
> — that's the change word. Loose coins, small notes, the stuff rattling in a pocket.

**ANNA:** The root is 'sill' — meaning small, scattered, minor. You hear it in 'sillai' too, a small thing, a trivial thing. Coimbatore people use it a little dismissively: sill-level stuff, not worth a meeting.

**ANNA:** சில்லறை
> literally leans toward 'the scattered small things'. Not one coin. The whole loose pile of them.

**ANNA:** அவசரம்
> — that's hurry. And this one has Sanskrit in it, which is unusual because Coimbatore Tamil is proud about not needing Sanskrit.

**ANNA:** 'Avashara' in Sanskrit means urgency, the state of needing immediately. Tamil absorbed it, softened the ending, and now it belongs to everyone's grandmother.

**ANNA:** But here's the thing they share: neither one is about a single moment. Sillai is a pile. Avasaram is a state. They're both words for a condition you're in, not a thing that happens once.

**ANNA:** When you say you have hurry, you're not describing an event. You're describing the room you're standing in right now.

## 36. lore — what 'room' really holds

**ANNA:** what 'room' really holds

**ANNA:** There is a word in Tamil that means room. But it also means something else, and that second meaning is older.

**ANNA:** அறை
> arai — the word

**ANNA:** The root is to cut. Arai is a cut-off space. Not a place you build — a place you divide off from the larger world.

**ANNA:** In Coimbatore, the older generation still use it for half. Half a coconut. Half a betel nut. The same word.

**ANNA:** அரை
> arai — half

**ANNA:** One letter different in the written form, same sound in the mouth. Your room is your half. The piece cut away from everything outside it.

**ANNA:** So when someone at the house calls you into a room to talk privately — there is already a concept in the word itself. This is the half that is not the world.

**ANNA:** தெரியுமா?
> you know this already, maybe
